Huawei, while presenting its Ascend 960DT AI accelerator to prospective customers early this month, asked them to source their own high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which has become essential infrastructure for training and running large-scale AI models. Its supply is currently dominated by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

That’s because companies in China find it hard to secure HBM supply due to U.S. export controls, and industry watchers believe AI companies in China are now running low on their HBM stockpiles. An AI accelerator’s performance depends not only on the compute die but also on the capacity and bandwidth of the HBM beside it.

Ascend 960DT, due in early 2027, aims to compete with H100-class accelerators in AI servers. After the U.S. government restricted exports of Nvidia’s GPUs and other advanced AI processors to China, Huawei’s Ascend AI chips have become the most widely used AI accelerators in China. Huawei plans to release at least one new Ascend processor each year through 2029.

A few weeks after news surfaced that Huawei was asking Ascend 960DT customers to buy HBM themselves, Bloomberg reports that Huawei researchers have developed a new HBM with twice the data-pin density of memory devices currently mass-produced by Samsung and SK Hynix. Huawei will present more details about this custom HBM at ISSCC 2027, held on Feb. 14-18, 2027, in San Francisco.

The new HBM features a 64-channel, 4096-DQ data interface, and 5-layer wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding, a 3D chip packaging technology that directly interconnects two full silicon wafers face-to-face without using any fillers between them. That, in turn, results in higher interconnect density, reduced power consumption and signal loss, and taller 3D die stacks.

In this custom HBM design, a five-layer direct-bond interconnection in HBM memory could refer to five stacked layers, with four DRAM layers connecting to the integrated memory controller via copper-to-copper or dielectric bonds. A paper scheduled for presentation at ISSCC 2027, titled “A 64-Channel 4096-DQ Custom HBM with Memory Controllers and 5-Layer Wafer-on-Wafer Hybrid Bonding,” describes how seven Huawei researchers based in Shenzhen plan to combine the memory controller with a multi-layer stacked memory design to build a customized memory framework.

Huawei has already used hybrid bonding in its Kirin mobile processors, which will launch later this year. In addition to hybrid bonding, Huawei’s HBM is also prioritizing thermal management and density optimization to address common bottlenecks in AI memory architecture.

ISSCC, an international conference hosted by the IEEE Solid-State Circuits Society and widely dubbed the Olympics of semiconductor design, requires designs implemented in actual silicon along with measurement results. However, it’s unclear how far Huawei has advanced in this HBM design undertaking amid massive design and manufacturing challenges.

No wonder memory industry experts in South Korea are watching this high-tech development closely. “Samsung Electronics is also developing various custom HBMs at a commercialization level with major U.S. big tech companies and applying hybrid bonding, and SK Hynix is doing the same,” said Choi Jae-hyuk, a professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University.

Kim Bong-jin, a professor in the School of Electrical Engineering at KAIST, acknowledged that HBM technology has advanced to the point where it’s difficult to distinguish the Samsung, SK Hynix, and CXMT papers. However, he noted that there is a difference between proving a technology in a paper and actually mass-producing a product.

In short, the key isn’t design metrics but mass production, and a considerable gap remains between proving a technology in a paper and supplying it reliably. So, while Huawei is seeking ways to break into the most lucrative AI hardware sector, it will most likely be an uphill battle for the Shenzhen, China-based tech behemoth to establish meaningful market share against entrenched competitors—Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix—with decades of memory fabrication expertise.

At the same time, however, sanctions on China’s technology firms actually drove them to innovate more. Huawei teasing an HBM device illustrates this geopolitical irony; Huawei’s Ascend processors have become the most popular AI accelerators in China after U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced GPUs.

data.title: Siemens Adds SoC Verification and Software Debug with Two Planned Deals
data.description:

A chip and the software that runs on it have to work together. Yet the engineering teams developing them have often operated separately, making that goal difficult to achieve.

Hardware and embedded software engineers have historically operated in separate groups, using separate tools, with problems sometimes emerging when their work finally comes together. As systems become more complex, the consequence of that late discovery becomes harder to afford.

Siemens’s proposed acquisitions of Breker Verification Systems and Lauterbach address different parts of that problem. Breker would expand its SoC verification capabilities; Lauterbach would bring embedded software debug and trace technology closer to its hardware verification tools. Together, the agreements extend Siemens’s effort to connect chip development with the software that makes the hardware useful.

For Laurie Balch, research director at EDA analyst firm Pedestal Research, the underlying pressure is straightforward: Engineers must check increasingly complicated designs without an unlimited supply of people to do it.

“Verification is struggling because it is such a big task,” Balch told EE Times. “And the complexity of the chips, the sheer size and magnitude of what is being fit into each chip makes verification very complex. There are so many moving parts; there are so many interconnected parts.”

Finding a problem earlier can avoid having to retrace development work later. Finding it after production—or after customers start using the product—raises the stakes further.

“You don’t want to have to get all the way down to production before you realize there are issues with your design and then have to backtrack through the process,” she said.

The two planned deals approach that challenge from different directions.

Bringing the pieces together

Siemens announced its agreement to acquire Breker on Nov. 17. The San Jose company develops technology that automates verification scenario generation, helping engineers check interactions among processors, memory, interconnects, software workloads, and other IP blocks. Its system verification IP and test suite synthesis would complement Siemens’s Questa One portfolio and existing verification IP. The transaction is expected to close in December 2026, subject to customary conditions; financial terms were not disclosed.

The engineering issue extends beyond whether individual components function correctly. Engineers also need to establish whether those components interact as intended, across the combinations of activity a complete SoC may encounter.

Balch sees Breker as a complementary addition to Siemens’s established strengths in checking designs and developing test capabilities. It also fits the industry’s effort to move more verification work earlier in development—the approach commonly called “shift left.”

Lauterbach brings a different engineering community into the picture.

Announced on Nov. 10, that agreement would add hardware-assisted debugging and real-time trace tools for embedded software. Siemens said combining those capabilities with its hardware-assisted verification technology would help developers examine hardware and software behavior together before a physical chip is available. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary conditions and regulatory approvals. Lauterbach, based near Munich, generated roughly €60 million (~$65.9 million) in revenue in 2025.

Balch draws a distinction between general application development and the embedded software work addressed by Lauterbach: software that runs directly on, and closely controls, the hardware.

“When you’re architecting the hardware, you’ve got to be thinking about the hardware and the software all at once,” she said.

That changes what a complete development process needs to accomplish. Each team can investigate its own work, yet still miss a problem that appears when software executes on the hardware.

The need is particularly acute in industries such as automotive and aerospace, where failures can have serious consequences. Balch said those industries have strong reasons to involve different engineering disciplines earlier and consider how their decisions affect one another.

“We in the industry have long talked about how the engineering teams are very much in individual silos historically and do their own thing separately,” she said. “They only come together at the very end. That’s a philosophy the industry has been trying to tackle and demolish for quite some time.”

She views the acquisitions as a continuation of Siemens’s direction since buying Mentor Graphics: connecting electronic design with a broader view of product engineering. Breker deepens its reach within chip verification, while Lauterbach extends its reach into the embedded software community.

Although Siemens’s Breker announcement emphasizes growing verification demands associated with AI, Balch sees a rationale that extends across product generations and applications.

“I think these are truly more fundamental acquisitions than AI,” she said.

The integration takes longer

The strategic fit leaves Siemens with a practical challenge: bringing the businesses together does not automatically give engineers a shared development environment.

Balch expects work beyond connecting products through APIs. Additional technology may be needed to address gaps between tools and improve how engineering work moves between them. Customers may also need help changing development methods that have long separated hardware from software.

Her longer-term vision is an environment in which both groups can examine the design together, with fewer barriers between their tools. She describes that as a direction of travel, rather than an immediate consequence of the transactions.

“I don’t expect that in the short term we’re going to see immediate changes to any of these products,” Balch said. “I think these are very long-term propositions.”

Part of the challenge is how companies regard software itself. The ability to change code after hardware has been manufactured has historically encouraged the assumption that software problems are less costly to fix.

Balch argued that assumption becomes less useful as software takes on more responsibility for product behavior. “Software redesign has tremendous cost involved in it,” she said. “And it can’t be viewed as a secondary phase of product design.”

In an automotive system, for example, correcting software may avoid rebuilding hardware, but deploying the correction still carries costs and can damage customers’ confidence. Earlier joint development is intended to reduce that exposure.

Even a more integrated offering will have to compete with engineers’ willingness to assemble their own toolchains. Balch said advanced development teams often accept the effort of connecting products from different suppliers when individual tools offer capabilities they need.

“For them, the effort involved in doing the integration themselves between leading-edge tools is worth it if they can have leading-edge capabilities in each of the separate areas of their design methodology,” she said.

She consequently expects the acquisitions to strengthen Siemens in areas where it already has a substantial presence and broaden its software reach, rather than immediately change its competitive ranking against Synopsys and Cadence.

“I think this is more about expanding the overall market than it is about taking market share from the other competitors,” Balch said.

The eventual evidence will come from engineering teams: How they use the tools, whether adoption grows, and whether customers report that the capabilities solve development problems.

“If customers are adopting the technologies, if they’re adopting the tools in greater numbers, that’s where we see the proof,” she said. “Because design engineers are not going to pay for tools they are not going to use.”

Siemens has identified more of the pieces it wants in its development portfolio. Customers will judge the combination by how much earlier it helps them discover that those pieces do—or do not—work together.

data.title: Bridging the Research-to-Manufacturing Gap in Canada’s Semiconductor Industry

Covering Canada’s semiconductor industry means getting familiar with the coun­try’s vast geography. From Vancouver’s particle beams to Saskatchewan’s mate­rials research, Ontario’s photonics, and Quebec’s quantum hardware, capabilities are separated by considerable distances. Geography also shapes what Canadian engineers build: systems that mon­itor remote waters, operate beneath Arctic ice, and conserve power far from reliable infrastructure. Connecting that expertise is as much a national challenge as developing it.

The opportunity is not to reproduce every semiconductor capability found elsewhere. It is to turn specialized strengths into globally competi­tive systems and companies. In my reporting for EE Times, optimism about Canada’s photonics, advanced packaging, and quantum capabilities comes with familiar concerns about capital, talent, and commercialization. Research excellence does not automatically become industrial capacity—or guarantee that its economic value stays in Canada.

Ottawa’s recent initiatives put scale closer to the center of that conversation. The Canadian Quantum Champions Program’s first phase provides up to C$92 million (~$65 million) in milestone-based contributions to Anyon Systems, Nord Quantique, Photonic, and Xanadu. The federal Defense Industrial Strategy connects quantum, AI, and emerging technolo­gies to sovereign capabilities, with the Bureau of Research, Engineering and Advanced Leadership in Innovation and Science (BOREALIS) coordinating defense innovation. The opportunity is to connect research with operational requirements and cus­tomers—not simply fund another demonstration.

Canada’s geography makes that connection particularly relevant. In Nova Scotia, sensing, communications, and low-power processing can serve fisheries research, environmental monitor­ing, and naval surveillance. Autonomous vehicles operating beneath Arctic ice need compact, rugged electronics that can sense, navigate, and conserve energy. Dual-use technology reflects overlapping engineering requirements, but turning that over­lap into business requires procurement pathways and supply chain access.

Quantum presents another scaling challenge. Xanadu is pursuing manufacturing partnerships, detector cooling, and photonics infrastructure alongside its computing architecture. Toronto-based startup Meissner Technologies uses AI-guided materials discovery to seek supercon­ductors that could ease photon-detector cooling requirements. Both illustrate the engineering requirements for bridging scientific promise and commercial deployment.

The supporting infrastructure stretches across the map. Saskatchewan combines quantum research, chip design talent, and materials charac­terization tools with plans for major AI computing capacity. Vancouver’s TRIUMF supplies specialized materials probes and radiation-testing facilities. Making these complementary resources accessible nationally for researchers and busi­nesses alike matters, alongside building the domestic computing infrastructure needed to capitalize on Canada’s AI expertise.

In this Special Report, we follow those connec­tions: coastal engineers building for unforgiving environments, laboratories investigating tomorrow’s materials, and quantum companies preparing for manufacturing and deployment. Can Canada turn distributed strengths and renewed government backing into durable industrial capa­bilities at home?

Located on Canada’s west coast, TRIUMF’s normal-conducting cyclotron, unique materials probes, and irradiation facilities serve everything from quantum materials and radiation-hardened electronics to medical isotopes.

data.title: EU Rules Bring New Safety Requirements for Farm Robots
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Digitalization and advancements in new technologies are making farming operations smarter, more automated, and more sustainable. But are these technologies explicitly safe to implement in agricultural settings?

There are already autonomous systems, including robots, drones, automated tractors, and AI-guided machines in the field that perform seed planting tasks, selective chemical spraying, mechanical weed control, milking, and feeding animals, and some prototype robots are now even picking apples in orchards. A lot of these are self-navigating and work with little-to-no human input.

These machines and robotic systems make farming operations more efficient and help reduce costs. But as machines ‘think’ and operate with less and less human input, an obvious question arises: Can they be trusted as much as when humans are fully in control?

The answer is not straightforward. While the technical aspects to consider are fairly well-established today, the definition of an autonomous system and who is responsible if something goes wrong is a lot more ambiguous and less clear-cut. Mandatory EU regulations coming into effect soon are set to quell this ambiguity and improve overall safety on farms where robots and other autonomous and AI-driven systems are part of everyday operations.

The AI and autonomous technologies being deployed

AI-driven and autonomous technologies are being deployed across a range of farming activities, from crop cultivation and soil analysis to irrigation management, fertilizer and pesticide spraying, weed removal, crop monitoring, field mapping, apple picking, and animal husbandry. Some tasks can be handled by a single robot, while others require a swarm of robots to cover a wider area. Applications include autonomous tractors that operate in fields at night, robotic sprayers that self-navigate rows of crops or trees, or a drone swarm overhead equipped with advanced sensors to monitor plant growth, identify growth-related problems, and spot potential threats to plant and soil health.

Many of these systems are driven by AI or have AI-enabled capabilities that help them navigate the field autonomously. AI allows these robotic and autonomous systems to process data a lot faster and handle larger volumes of data than systems without AI or machine learning (ML). This enables more efficient planning, earlier detection of potential problems before they become a big issue (including issues that might have otherwise been missed), and predictive capabilities that support a wide array of farming operations. However, replacing human workers in the field with AI-enabled machines doesn’t mean that there are fewer risks; it simply introduces different risks that need to be taken into account.

Lack of clarity could bring safety risks

Autonomous systems operating in the field face a number of inherent technical risks. What if fail-safes stop working and the robot hits a person? What if collision-free navigation is impacted by misaligned sensor fusion or dust on the sensor? Will the uneven terrain affect the locomotion and stability of some robots, making them unsafe?

Many of these technical aspects have been addressed, but anchoring the safety of autonomous systems in standards and regulations requires a lot more clarity around what an autonomous system actually is. More clarity is also needed on responsibility. Autonomous systems equipped with AI do not remove responsibility from the farm if something goes wrong, so farmers need clearer guidance and must understand that they are not immune to safety infractions if the technology goes awry.

The current EU Machinery Directive and harmonized standards, such as ISO 12100:2010, do not use the term ‘autonomous’. As with ‘artificial intelligence’, the term ‘autonomous’ is open to interpretation, and European regulations have suffered the same fate, with many different interpretations of what an ‘autonomous’ system is. In the automotive sector, there is a sliding scale created by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE), which has been widely adopted across industries, ranging from Level 0 to Level 5 based on the degree of driving automation. Therefore, one person’s perception of autonomy may be different from someone else’s.

Autonomy is typically defined in terms of the activity and behavior of a machine. There is also the argument that a machine is always automated because the activities are carried out by the machine regardless of whether there has been human input or not. More complex tasks typically require some level of human oversight, whereas more basic tasks do not.

To make automated machines safe, accountable, and responsible in the field, understanding what constitutes autonomy—and what doesn’t—is an important distinction that needs to be clarified through closer scrutiny. If machines are still meant to have human oversight, but workers allow them to operate on their own because they are ‘autonomous’, it could lead to various safety issues and hazardous situations.

So, a greater degree of clarity will enable farmers and their workers to better understand which systems can be left on their own with minimal oversight and which systems need more robust monitoring and oversight to ensure that all automated and semi-automated operations in the field remain safe and hazard-free.

For situations where humans are not responsible for oversight and spotting hazardous situations, the operating environment needs to be designed so that hazards don’t manifest, or there needs to be a separate monitoring system (such as a machine learning-based system or overhead drone imaging) in place to spot hazards and alert the autonomous robots/vehicles before they encounter them. Knowing which systems need this level of design and which don’t because humans will be looking over them is not only relevant from a safety perspective but also from a cost and infrastructure perspective, as the extra technology should only be installed where it is needed (as it increases the complexity of farming infrastructure).

How new European policies are looking to make autonomous farming safer

There are a couple of new regulations coming within the EU that should help clarify the ‘what is an autonomous machine’ situation and how they are deployed safely in the field. The first is the new EU 2023/1230 regulation on machinery. Although it came into effect in 2023, it will apply to all EU member states from Jan. 20, 2027, replacing the Machinery Directive that has governed machinery since 2006.

This regulation includes ‘autonomous mobile machinery’, which it defines in relation to machinery that performs safety functions while moving and operating without continuous operator intervention.

The regulation covers certain categories of machinery incorporating safety components with fully or partially self-evolving, machine-learning-based behavior that ensure safety functions, and machinery with embedded systems of this kind. These are listed in Annex I, Part A of the regulation and require conformity assessment by a notified body. This does not mean that all machinery using AI or ML is automatically classified as high risk or requires third-party certification.

But the regulation goes beyond this. Where relevant, autonomous mobile machinery will need to have a mandatory ‘supervisory function’ related to the autonomous mode, which will allow the machine to be stopped or started remotely to move it to a safe place where it cannot create further risk. If autonomous systems do not include this, they will no longer be compliant. However, machinery lawfully placed on the market before Jan. 20, 2027, stays lawful. The obligation applies to new machinery placed on the market from that date.

Farm owners also need to evaluate any risks when buying the equipment, especially AI technology, and be aware of any updates, changes, and new risk assessments released by the manufacturer. Finally, autonomous machines also need to log and store all data in case there is an accident or safety incident, as this increases transparency and accountability of the autonomous systems used on the farm.

The other key act is the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This came into effect on Aug. 1, 2024, and became generally applicable on Aug. 2, 2026. Compliance requirements are being added for high-risk AI systems in agricultural vehicles. This was initially planned for August 2027, but the deadline has recently been moved to Aug. 2, 2028. In this context, not all AI systems used in machinery are automatically classified as high risk. Under the EU AI Act, classification depends on specific criteria, including whether the AI system is a safety component of a regulated product under EU product safety law or is a regulated product itself, or whether the machine requires third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the EU market.

Machinery that is deemed to be high risk under EU product safety laws must meet requirements for transparency, documentation, and human oversight. Farmers who deploy high-risk AI systems will have to use them in line with the manufacturer’s instructions and implement human oversight.

These changes mean that farmers are going to need to be more robust in their documentation and compliance with stricter guidelines. This is going to include more formal risk assessments, maintaining stricter records, defining operating zones and protocols to ensure that autonomous machines work within clear and strict boundaries, and training staff to monitor the machinery and react if there is an incident. All these procedures will help to make farms that use autonomous machines safer.

These new regulations represent important steps toward defining autonomous systems and establishing the measures farms will need to put in place to keep personnel, visitors, and the robots themselves safe. The onus on workplace safety, however, has not changed. Farmers have been responsible for the safety of their personnel, and the onus is still on the farm to keep their workers safe even if the technology operates without direct human control. While the regulations go some way to improving the safety of autonomous machines in smart farms, there are still challenges to sort out about the allocation of liability if there is a failure with a machine. As regulations evolve alongside emerging and maturing technologies, it is almost certain that other issues and edge cases will be addressed in the coming years.

data.title: AI Makes Formal Verification Practical
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

LONDON, U.K. — Math AI foundation model startup Harmonic is expanding into formal verification for software and hardware, starting with C, Verilog, and Rust.

Formal verification is a well-known technique for proving code is correct, and when extended to hardware description languages such as Verilog, for proving hardware designs are correct and will function exactly as the specification demands. Though it’s well known, formal verification is used in a relatively limited way today, and only by specialists, Harmonic CEO Tudor Achim told EE Times.

There are two main techniques used for formal verification today. Most existing schemes use model checkers, which run the code many times over to explore all the possible states to try to find a state for which the code doesn’t behave as intended. Model checkers are powerful, but as the complexity of hardware increases, they are increasingly compute-intensive.

The other method, theorem proving, creates a logical proof that the implementation of the code is mathematically equivalent to its specification. Until now, this required humans to write proofs, and was very difficult for complex hardware.

“Historically, theorem proving has been horrible compared to model checkers,” Achim said. “Because to write a theorem proving proof, you need to write a lot of language, and to write a model checking proof you just need to solve some very specific algorithmic math problems.”

Computers have historically been good at solving specific problems, such as those in model checking, but unsuitable for tackling unstructured problems such as writing proofs. AI has changed everything, Achim said.

“With AI, computers are now unbelievably good at writing unstructured things. So now theorem proving which had no promise for 50 years now has all the promise, because it’s very scalable, if you can write down the right proof,” he said.

Trained for math

An AI model trained for math, such as Harmonic’s Aristotle, can be applied to solve this type of proof. Aristotle has been trained using reinforcement learning over a period of two years, recently achieving gold-medal equivalent performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad.

Hardware and software are not handled differently by Aristotle; C or Verilog code is compiled via Harmonic’s proprietary compilers into a math problem, which is given to Aristotle to solve. Harmonic’s IP is in both turning the problem into math and solving that math, Achim said.

“It’s easy to vibe code a compiler that turns [code] into a math problem, but it’s hard to do one that’s actually correct across all the code on GitHub or can handle 30-million-gate designs,” he said. “There’s a lot of infrastructure [required] to actually do the proofs with this technology. You also need some models that are fast and cheap at doing it, because to write a proof of some code you probably need 10 to 100× as much code in the proof script as is in the original code.”

The actual theorem proving isn’t difficult, Achim said; in fact, it’s very simple compared to the hardest math problems.

“All it’s doing is what a smart developer would do — they have a mental model of what are the inputs to my function, what does my function do to it, and what’s the output,” he said. “You can think of it as really elaborate bookkeeping of the program state — there’s a lot more stuff you’re writing down for bookkeeping than in the code itself.”

This “elaborate bookkeeping” might be used to, for example, prove that there is no set of inputs to the chip that would result in deadlock. A natural-language statement gets turned into a mathematical theorem (written in Lean, a programming language invented for math), and the AI solves that theorem. The idea is to effectively build a model of what happens when the chip runs and prove for all possible inputs that a certain condition can’t happen. If it fails, the AI can produce a counterexample — perhaps a waveform for a particular set of conditions that results in deadlock.

This technique can be used to find bugs very deep in the design. AI chip company Tensordyne, a Harmonic customer, used Aristotle to find bugs more than 100,000 cycles deep, multiple orders of magnitude beyond what model checkers could have found, according to Achim.

How big a design can Aristotle handle?

“We’re at probably a million FLOPS and 20 million to 30 million gates right now, so still not quite full CPU scale,” Achim said. “Empirically, we have scaled the size of designs we can handle by 10x every two and a half months, and we see that continuing, so I think by the middle or end of next year, we’d ideally be at full CPU scale.”

In practice, Aristotle typically runs on blocks of the design, and theorems that have been proven for individual blocks can be reused to prove things about other blocks that depend on them, Achim said. This technique can be used to verify arbitrarily large designs.

The size limitation for single runs is the size of the proof scripts, which are orders of magnitude bigger than the original code, and the artifacts these scripts generate, which are even larger. Eventually, the infrastructure just isn’t big enough.

“Ultimately it becomes a data management question and a parallelization question,” Achim said.

There are also human factors that limit the size of designs that can be verified in a single run.

“As you approach larger designs, you start to run into limitations of the clarity of the specification the designer made — there might be assumptions baked in that are not clear,” Achim said. “A formal analysis is the most detailed analysis of a chip, and it forces you to have all your assumptions out in the open. Traditionally, teams have not been forced to do that.”

With AI, the ability to prove theorems is today outstripping humans’ ability to write specifications, especially as designs get more complex, Achim said.

AI-driven workflows

Formal verification has been used at the end of a workflow to ensure the design is correct before tape-out, but with the dawn of AI-driven workflows, Aristotle could be used during the design process as the specifications evolve with the design, testing that all the properties still hold for every revision, Achim said.

“What we see across the board is that people are rethinking what their flow looks like,” he said. “The old flow was very human-centric; you had well-integrated tools across the board, but people now want to develop at the speed of agents, and I don’t know that people are as wedded to their workflows as one might have thought a year ago.”

Many customers are using agents to assist with designs and write code, but verifying hardware (and software) has been a stubborn holdout for automation so far, Achim said. Automating formal verification could therefore be another step toward removing humans from the chip design process entirely.

Achim expects that easier, scalable formal verification will change the economics of chip design too, since it should make large chip designs approachable even for small teams. “Historically a lot of money in chip development has gone toward verification, 70% to 80% by some estimates,” he said. “Even if you’re spending that much, you’re still limited in what you can be sure is correct, so I think people stayed away from super complex and weird designs … but once you have formal verification and correctness, I think all bets are off.”

In the current memory-hungry, AI-driven landscape, severe supply constraints have driven prices to all-time highs, even when supply is available. With demand continuing to grow and supply unlikely to catch up for at least the next two years, if not longer, and no significant breakthroughs in memory technology on the horizon, the industry is looking for ways to use available memory more efficiently. The good news is that AMD might have just found a solution.

Solving the memory crisis

MEXT, a software company that AMD worked with and later acquired, found that much of the RAM in any given system is often wasted, with DRAM often overprovisioned, stranded, and underused. When analyzing RAM usage, MEXT found that 50% to 80% of memory pages in RAM are stale and have not been accessed by compute resources for more than five minutes. Those pages, known as cold pages, are kept there just in case they are needed again. Addressing this inefficiency is the basis of the solution AMD announced earlier this month.

At the recent AMD In Depth 2026 event in Las Vegas, the company announced AMD MEXT, a software solution designed to make better use of RAM by leveraging flash storage as a “parking lot” for memory pages until they are needed and brought back into RAM. This solution requires no hardware or software modifications to existing deployments and will be available alongside AMD EPYC CPUs.

Flash is a form of memory that is significantly cheaper and much more power efficient than DRAM. However, it is not typically used for active workloads because it is 500× slower than DRAM. To clear that roadblock, AMD MEXT uses AI to mitigate flash memory latency by transparently offloading cold pages to flash and having AI predict and push soon-to-be-needed pages back to the DRAM. This process relies on an ensemble of AI models, with continuous training performed in real time using only one AMD EPYC core, without requiring a GPU. The key is for MEXT to anticipate the next needed set of memory pages in a prediction window that is slightly longer than the latency of the flash storage being used. This allows MEXT to transparently leverage flash as DRAM.

A key focus during AMD’s briefing was the higher performance per DRAM dollar that MEXT can deliver in applications such as agentic AI and EDA, database and analytics, and media and entertainment. As shown in the image below, AMD’s internal benchmarks revealed that performance per DRAM dollar was as high as 3.5× using MEXT compared to strictly using DRAM in agentic AI benchmarks.

Using less DRAM to achieve the same performance at a lower cost is not the only potential benefit that AMD MEXT brings to the table. AMD MEXT can also be used to increase performance by up to 3× with the same amount of DRAM by effectively increasing the efficiency of that DRAM. This provides a much cheaper option than adding more DRAM for memory-intensive workloads. For example, AMD claims that MEXT can deliver 1.4× higher throughput in EDA workloads compared with a baseline DRAM configuration of the same capacity. This capability is vital for systems, as often the roadblock to obtaining more DRAM is not the cost of the DRAM, but rather its availability at scale.

Since MEXT can be used in both greenfield and brownfield deployments, real-world performance anywhere close to these published numbers would allow it to effectively address this bottleneck and simultaneously tackle both the cost and availability constraints that DRAM currently faces.

Tirias Research’s take

Currently, AMD MEXT is limited to data center and enterprise workloads, but if it performs as advertised, it is a revolutionary approach that has the potential to change not only the AI landscape but also applications across a wider range of devices that use RAM, including those in consumer and embedded workloads. Early signs indicate that this is the case: AMD has begun to implement MEXT internally, and according to the company, it has already saved $4.9 million on DRAM costs across 145 initial servers, with the intent to scale out to 2,000 servers in 2027.

While the company did not disclose MEXT’s licensing structure, the cost will certainly be far lower than the cost to purchase the equivalent amount of DRAM, assuming it is even available. Even if prices were to normalize, which will not happen for the next few years at the earliest, this solution will have far-reaching implications for the long-term AI cost basis, which is already starting to produce sticker shock across multiple industries.

Winbond Electronics is betting that a little less customization will put its 3D-stacked memory architecture into a lot more designs, while expanding its 16-nm DRAM portfolio and adding security certification to NOR flash offerings.

The company’s new CUBE-Lite is a semi-custom memory offering derived from its Customized Ultra Bandwidth Elements (CUBE) platform, which debuted a few years ago. It aims to give edge AI designs CUBE’s bandwidth with lower non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs than a fully customized CUBE design.

“It’s still customized, but it’s more of a ‘standardized’ customized, if that’s not too much of a contradiction,” Brian Watson, marketing manager for Winbond’s customized memory solutions, said in a briefing with EE Times.

CUBE works best for workloads with low-to-medium density requirements but high bandwidth requirements, he said. Rather than replicate high-bandwidth memory’s combination of capacity and bandwidth, Winbond is targeting smaller working sets that still require rapid data movement. “It’s not trying to mimic HBM in terms of both density and bandwidth, but just the bandwidth.”

Watson offered on-device language translation in a wearable as a hypothetical example. The audio-processing working set might be relatively small, but responsiveness requires bandwidth. These types of devices are cost sensitive, he added. “You might not be able to amortize the NRE cost of a fully custom 3D-stacked memory architecture across the number of devices that you’re selling in the unit price of the device.”

CUBE-Lite delivers up to 8 GB/s of memory bandwidth at approximately 70 mW, and Winbond’s engineering data shows the simplified interface can reduce SoC controller power consumption by more than 10× compared with an LPDDR4X implementation.

A full CUBE design is tailored to each customer’s bandwidth, density, power, and SoC requirements. CUBE-Lite instead offers a menu of density and I/O options—Watson used 128, 256, and 512 I/Os as hypothetical examples. “It wouldn’t be fully customized, right, because you would have to select among the available options,” he said. CUBE-Lite also requires the customer to provide a memory controller.

Filling DRAM density gaps

Winbond is also expanding its 16-nm DRAM portfolio with 8-Gb LPDDR4 devices with an x16 interface, 16-Gb LPDDR4 with an x32 interface, and 16-Gb DDR4. The additions fill density gaps and give customers more options across product tiers.

The 16-Gb devices double per-device capacity compared with 8-Gb parts, potentially reducing component counts and board space. DDR4 targets include switches and server peripherals, while LPDDR4 applications include automotive systems, drones, and surveillance equipment. The new 16-Gb products are scheduled for availability by year-end 2026, with mass production planned for the second quarter of 2027.

Securing NOR flash with CRA

Separately, Winbond introduced a Cyber Resilience Act Conformance and Integration Kit for its TrustME W77Q Secure Flash family. The package combines hardware security, software, integration guidance, testing resources, and documentation to support manufacturers’ product-level compliance work.

In a briefing with EE Times, Nir Tasher, VP of technology for Winbond’s secure memory products, said many equipment suppliers lack the security expertise needed to translate regulatory requirements into implementations. Supplying silicon and a data sheet alone does not address that gap, he said.

The W77Q’s SESIP Level 2 certification can help manufacturers document component security, but it does not establish CRA conformity for the finished product, Tasher said.

Instead, the kit maps CRA requirements to Secure Flash features. It also includes sample code, a test suite to verify integration, and the written collateral needed for conformance documentation. “This is like a secret sauce,” Tasher said. “You add that to your system, and you are 90% of the way there.”

Those resources, together with documentation, allow customers to move through conformance work more efficiently, he said.

W77Q has achieved SESIP Level 2 certification, though Winbond notes that this alone doesn’t establish a finished product’s conformity with the CRA. Tasher said other regions, including the U.S. and Japan, could follow the EU’s regulatory approach.

Winbond to absorb Infineon memory business

The trio of product updates follows Winbond’s September agreement to acquire Infineon Technologies’ NOR Flash and F-RAM business in an all-cash transaction valued at $1.12 billion.

Winbond will operate the business as a standalone entity headquartered in Silicon Valley. Infineon will retain its SRAM, HYPERRAM, nvSRAM, and SONOS-based radiation-hardened memory products. Subject to regulatory approvals, the companies are targeting closing in the second half of 2027.

Neither Winbond nor Infineon was willing to discuss the transaction beyond the news release.

data.title: The Enigma of SoftBank’s $1 Trillion SK Hynix Buyout Attempt
data.description:

SK Hynix, the world’s second-largest memory chipmaker, is in the news again, this time for being the target of a trillion-dollar buyout attempt by the Japanese tech conglomerate SoftBank. According to a report published in The Information on Friday (Nov. 20), SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son recently explored a $1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix.

A SoftBank spokesperson responded in a short statement: “SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration.” SK Hynix said the company had no knowledge of the matter and that any outreach happened entirely on the SoftBank side.

Apparently, Son sounded out a $1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix and then shelved it. The most likely hurdles could be financing, chaebol governance, and the Korean Government’s view of the memory industry as a strategic asset. The latter makes it a deal that could never close anyway. And there were no negotiations or a term sheet.

But that’s only half the story. Especially when the report didn’t establish Son’s specific rationale for choosing SK Hynix. For starters, the trillion-dollar figure is far higher than SK’s $577 billion market valuation recorded on Friday, Nov. 20. So, the floated trillion-dollar price is 1.7× SK Hynix’s current market value.

The largest tech industry acquisition on record is SpaceX’s $250 billion takeover of xAI in 2026, combining aerospace, satellite, and AI operations. Moreover, SoftBank’s balance sheet is already stretched by its AI bets on OpenAI and Stargate; it recently sold its entire Nvidia stake to raise cash. It’s also mobilizing its stake in Arm to secure funding for investments in OpenAI and Stargate.

So, the question is how SoftBank would arrange the sheer scale of this trillion-dollar funding. In retrospect, it looks more like a financing inquiry. There were no price negotiations and no indications of commitments from Wall Street banks. In other words, it wasn’t a takeover attempt, but an early-stage exploration.

More importantly, there is literally no chance that the Korean Government would approve such a deal. Furthermore, while Korean Government approval is almost unimaginable, SK Hynix has no reason to sell either. That makes this whole episode a non-starter. So, what’s this fuss all about? If Masayoshi Son didn’t actually want to buy SK Hynix, what would he gain from this buyout story, for which he paid nothing?

What Son wants

Industry observers believe this buyout attempt signals Son’s grand plan to build an AI empire, which requires owning every layer of the value chain. Start with Arm, which sits at the semiconductor design IP layer. It controls chip designs that underpin a range of AI processors; furthermore, Arm’s neutral licensing platform effectively serves the entire chip design industry.

Next, SoftBank snapped Graphcore in 2024 and Ampere Computing in 2025, the two upstarts developing AI processors. The Japanese conglomerate has also acquired a significant stake in Intel. At the model layer, powered by AI processors, SoftBank has committed a massive investment in OpenAI.

At the AI infrastructure level, SoftBank has poured nearly $500 billion into the Stargate joint venture and the acquisition of data center investor DigitalBridge. The Japanese giant is also the largest shareholder in SB Energy, which runs data center and power businesses.

What’s missing here is memory, which has become a chokepoint in the AI buildout. In fact, memory suppliers have become more important to the companies designing AI accelerators and building data centers to run them. And on SoftBank’s AI buildup map, one layer is empty: memory.

It’s worth mentioning that SK Hynix is a pioneer in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which enables processors to handle the vast volumes of data required for AI computing. In 2025, SK Hynix’s HBM revenue more than doubled year on year. Nvidia is SK Hynix’s largest customer, accounting for 14.8% of its revenue in the first quarter of 2026, and according to TrendForce, Nvidia is expected to place about two-thirds of its HBM4 orders with SK Hynix.

Apparently, by owning a major memory chipmaker, SoftBank could extend its reach across the AI supply chain. So, it’s probably a precursor to SoftBank buying a partial stake in a memory chipmaker or buying the whole company outright.

SK Hynix isn’t up for sale, and Son doesn’t need to buy it because even a hostile takeover bid isn’t realistic. But Son tested the financial appetite for bankrolling an acquisition of a memory chipmaker and then walked away. After this free due diligence, if he buys a partial stake in a memory company or buys the whole company for much less, it will look like a concession.

data.title: Pat Gelsinger Goes Hunting for Europe’s Unbuilt Tech Companies
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Europe cannot simply spend its way back into the conventional race for leading-edge logic, according to Pat Gelsinger.

“If you want to go compete on 14A, the starting point is 50 years of lithography expertise and $50 billion,” the former Intel CEO told EE Times. “Otherwise, don’t show up for the race.”

It sounds like an argument for surrender. Gelsinger, now a general partner at deep-tech venture firm Playground Global, means almost the opposite. The semiconductor industry may be dominated by a shrinking number of companies capable of financing its most advanced processes, but he believes the basis of competition is beginning to change.

“In the next phase, as we see it, the entire stack changes,” Gelsinger said.

That change is why Playground Global formed a partnership with French research organization CEA. Announced in July, the memorandum of understanding covers advanced computing, microelectronics, AI, quantum technologies, energy, and biotechnology. It pairs CEA’s researchers and infrastructure with Playground’s capital, company building experience, and international network.

Put less formally, Gelsinger has come to Europe looking for companies that do not exist yet.

Companies made from “raw cloth”

Playground Global calls itself an early-stage investor, but that description doesn’t quite capture how early it’s willing to arrive.

“In a number of cases, we’re forming companies out of pretty raw cloth,” Gelsinger said.

The firm searches laboratories, universities, and research institutes for technologies that could become the foundation of a company. It may encounter only a pair of researchers, a scientific result, and a rough sense that something important has become possible.

Playground then helps recruit executives, define the market, build the business, navigate government relationships, and raise subsequent rounds of capital. It normally takes a board seat, and, in some cases, portfolio companies place commercial staff inside Playground’s Silicon Valley facility.

“Some venture capitalists are very hands-off,” Gelsinger said. “We are absolutely hands-on.”

The firm focuses on areas including new computing architectures, materials, biology, energy, and manufacturing. In May, it announced a $475 million fourth fund for early-stage deep-tech investments.

The attraction of CEA is therefore not difficult to understand. Its laboratories contain precisely the sort of difficult, expensive, and initially ambiguous technologies that conventional venture investors may struggle to evaluate.

The more interesting question is whether those technologies can escape the laboratory.

From lab to fab—and then to market

Julie Galland, director of CEA’s Technological Research Division, described CEA’s mission as taking technology “from lab to fab.” That means more than demonstrating that an idea works. Researchers must turn it into something that can be manufactured, transferred to an established industrial company, or built into a startup.

The agreement is broader than CEA-Leti, Galland emphasized. Leti is the CEA research institute specializing in microelectronics and digital technologies, but the partnership extends across other parts of CEA, drawing on capabilities in areas including energy and healthcare.

It also represents something new for CEA. Galland said this is the organization’s first dedicated partnership of its kind with a U.S. venture capital firm, although roughly 20% of CEA’s industrial partnerships are with American companies.

CEA already has technology transfer programs, industrial partnerships, and mechanisms for supporting spinouts. What Playground brings is access to the networks surrounding a global technology business: potential executives, suppliers, customers, partners, and later-stage investors.

CEA’s startups may originate in France, Galland said, but “their ambition is to be global.”

A startup needs technology, skills, a business plan, and money. It also needs to understand the value chain it’s about to enter—who will supply it, who might buy from it, and how to reach those people. Playground’s U.S. network and company building experience are intended to fill some of those gaps.

A steering committee will review opportunities quarterly. The traffic is designed to flow in both directions: CEA can present prospective spinouts to Playground, while Playground can connect its existing portfolio companies with CEA researchers, equipment, and development programs.

Rasheed Auguste, an investor at Playground with a background in nuclear engineering and the U.S. Department of Energy, will help apply the firm’s filter to prospective projects.

“Is the technology hard enough that most people won’t attempt it?” Auguste said. “Is the market large enough that it matters?”

Those questions exclude incremental improvements, even technically impressive ones. Playground is looking for technologies capable of changing an existing market or creating a new one—and therefore producing the scale of return required by venture capital.

Auguste called it the “Playground gauntlet.”

When old fabs meet new physics

The collaboration rests on a particular bet about the semiconductor industry: The next important computing platform may not emerge solely from smaller transistors.

Gelsinger pointed to cryogenic computing, quantum technology, photonics, superconducting devices, and new materials as examples of fields in which the rules remain unsettled. Some may depend on physical phenomena that conventional computing has barely exploited.

That could change which manufacturing assets matter. A mature semiconductor process combined with unfamiliar materials or devices may become more valuable than its feature size suggests.

“Now, all of a sudden, the 28-nm process technology with new material science may be the new winner,” Gelsinger said.

This is the opening he sees for Europe. The region may not control the most advanced logic processes, but it has research institutes, scientists, industrial expertise, and specialized infrastructure. If computing moves into a period of architectural and materials experimentation, those assets could matter more.

Playground portfolio company Snowcap offers an early example. Its work in superconducting computing has already created links with CEA, giving both organizations a model for how the broader partnership might operate.

Galland sees photonics following a similar trajectory. Optical technology is moving beyond communication between components and deeper into computing systems. “Some of my teams are dreaming about photonics in the computer,” she said.

The dream is technically alluring: Light could eventually play roles now performed by electrical signals, possibly addressing limitations in bandwidth and power. But the distance between a laboratory result and a dependable product remains vast. Crossing it requires capital, equipment, customers, and time.

That’s where the partnership encounters its most politically sensitive question.

The sovereignty problem

European governments want sovereign technology capabilities, strategic manufacturing, and more companies headquartered on the continent. Playground wants to build businesses for global markets—and its capital carries no guarantee that a company emerging from a French laboratory will remain French.

“Some of those companies that may emerge may be French-based or maybe domiciled elsewhere,” Gelsinger said.

A technology may originate at CEA, employ French researchers, and benefit from French public investment, yet ultimately be incorporated, financed, or expanded somewhere else. The same network that helps it become global could also loosen its connection to Europe.

Galland does not see global ambition and European sovereignty as irreconcilable. The French government understands that strategic technologies operate in international markets, she said, while CEA and its partners still seek investment, employment, and industrial activity in France.

“There is no inconsistency between these needs,” she said.

But clearly, there’s a negotiation. Playground is not a regional development agency, and CEA is not simply a source of intellectual property for Silicon Valley. Each wants something from the other.

“We think the best companies serve global markets,” Auguste said.

For Playground, that means looking wherever the underlying science is strongest and connecting it to customers and capital across borders. For CEA, it means using those connections without allowing globalization to become a one-way extraction of European research.

A long search

Gelsinger does not expect the partnership’s most important result to appear within Playground’s current $475 million investment fund, known as Fund IV—or perhaps even within the next fund.

Some CEA projects may be ready for investment relatively soon. Others will require years of maturation, while still others may reveal commercial possibilities that neither side can yet describe.

“So that’ll be the one past Fund 4,” Gelsinger said, “and the one past that, and the one past that.”

That may be the partnership’s most consequential feature. Playground is not merely shopping for startups that CEA has already prepared. It wants a position early enough to influence which technologies become companies, which markets they pursue, and how they enter the world.

Europe’s next major computing company may not begin by attempting to replicate today’s winners. It may begin with an overlooked material, an old process node, an unfamiliar piece of physics—and two researchers who do not yet realize they’re running a company.

Gelsinger has come to help them build one.

Palo Alto Networks, a cloud company that repositioned itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, has ventured into AI infrastructure by acquiring a startup with a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models. Applied Compute, co-founded in early 2025 by three former OpenAI researchers, grew from zero revenue to over $100 million in annual revenue in under 18 months while working with major AI companies.

Palo Alto Networks has announced it will acquire Applied Compute in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion. This acquisition caught the market by surprise not only because of its price tag, but also because Applied Compute operates outside the traditional cybersecurity sector.

First and foremost, the deal reflects a broader strategic shift in which major technology companies are now seeking to develop their own AI capabilities and gain greater control over AI systems, rather than relying solely on models from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Applied Compute specializes in post-training and inference infrastructure for open-weight AI models, which enables organizations to customize and deploy AI systems for specific applications.

Palo Alto Networks gets AI

Applied Compute helps companies adapt and run open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released. Apparently, they present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage, and misuse by bad actors. Post-training data is usually a company’s most confidential material—tickets, contracts, and customer records—and the adapted weights can retain fragments of it.

As a result, the model can inherit its training-set classification, so it can be traced and retired when a source is withdrawn. “Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO.

Catharine Trebnick, senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, told Reuters that AI tools are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than companies can patch them, pushing companies to consolidate onto fewer platforms. This deal, for instance, could allow Palo Alto Networks to develop cybersecurity-specialized models.

As the company moves into enterprise AI infrastructure with the acquisition of CyberArk, expected to close in the third quarter of 2027, it could embed security directly where enterprises train, govern, and run custom open-weight models. The question is why didn’t Palo Alto Networks build this technology with in-house engineering talent? A simple answer: Palo Alto Networks has engineers, but it doesn’t have time.

AI models embedding security

The deal signals a deeper integration of advanced AI capabilities into mainstream security products. It comes as a heightened threat environment pushes organizations toward broader security solutions. “Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to Palo Alto Networks, already at the center of many companies’ firewalls, chips, and identity controls,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research.

This acquisition could further spur consolidation in the cybersecurity AI space at a time when companies bolster their AI offerings. Especially when AI talent is still scarce within large security firms; it largely sits in small startup firms. Palo Alto Networks evaluated nine providers before settling on Applied Compute.

The acquisition also marks a shift in Palo Alto Networks’ strategy as AI reshapes both the cybersecurity market and enterprise technology’s infrastructure requirements. Palo Alto Networks is positioning itself not only to secure the growing use of AI models and autonomous agents, but also to provide some of the technology required to train, adapt, and run those models.

In other words, the deal will put Palo Alto Networks in a position to train, adapt, and deploy open-weight AI securely in both public cloud and sovereign cloud environments. As Gogia noted, while Palo Alto Networks has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys, none of that yet extends to AI accelerators.

Eventually, Palo Alto Networks aims to offer ⁠a technology platform that helps organizations securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI. This is especially true when no one is currently offering secure open-weight models. TD Cowen analyst Shaul Eyal summed it up by saying Applied Compute ⁠extends Palo Alto’s push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI.

The $4.5 billion transaction is subject to regulatory approval and other customary conditions and is expected to close during the third quarter of 2027. Once the transaction is complete, Yash Patil, co-founder and CEO of Applied Compute, will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks.

data.title: Memory R&D Is a High-Stakes Game
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The need for significant investment in R&D is nothing new for memory makers, but Micron Technology’s creation of a dedicated facility that looks beyond the next node illustrates why the industry cannot afford to skimp on R&D, especially in the AI era.

Micron Research Labs, announced in the summer of 2026, gives the DRAM maker a long-term research home of its own. Based in Boise, Idaho, and backed by a planned $10 billion investment over the next decade, the facility will focus on critical memory technologies, advanced memory and compute architectures, packaging, and future semiconductor manufacturing. The investment also covers university collaborations, satellite labs, and ecosystem partnerships.

Micron expects to break ground in 2027 on a facility capable of hosting hundreds of researchers. It has already appointed Deirdre Hanford, who spent 37 years at Synopsys, as corporate VP and president of the new lab. Hanford will lead the establishment of the lab’s research infrastructure, operating model, and partnerships.

The lab’s first notable outreach came earlier this fall, when Micron said it intends to invest up to $50 million over five years to support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission Graduate Fellowship Pilot Program and related national laboratory research.

For Scott DeBoer, Micron’s recently appointed president and chief technology and products officer, the lab represents a change in how the company participates in semiconductor research. The need for R&D has always been pressing, but efforts have mainly focused on relatively near-term challenges and goals, he said in an interview with EE Times. “I couldn’t have imagined the R&D investment level that we’re at today.”

DeBoer said the lab’s funding is an addition to previously announced or forecasted investments, which have increased significantly every year over the past four years.

Looking beyond the roadmap

Micron has always had to look ahead, DeBoer said, but mostly within the bounds of the company’s technology roadmaps, which usually chart the next five to seven years. “We have to have a pretty good view of what we’re investing in and what we’re going to bring to market through that period of time.”

He said the company has had less influence on research that looks a decade ahead or beyond, in part because there was more government funding flowing into U.S. universities. “We actually didn’t have to be the leader of that kind of research effort.” Now that memory has become much more important, Micron is taking more of a leadership role in longer-term research with universities and national labs, DeBoer said.

Micron’s approach in recent years emphasized supporting professors and students in building workforce capacity. Longer-horizon partnerships allow it to pursue foundational research outcomes while mitigating some of the intellectual property complications associated with projects nearing commercialization. “This is a pivot, where we go out farther, where we actually can have research outcomes in mind,” DeBoer said.

AI adds to the R&D burden

Much of the memory industry’s R&D has historically focused on immediate process and manufacturing improvements—shrinking DRAM from one node to the next and getting yields up. AI makes that longer view more urgent while complicating nearer-term development.

DeBoer said memory is the engine driving AI, whether in the data center or at the edge, in cars and robots, all of which depend heavily on memory performance, memory bandwidth, and power.

He said the diversity of applications is a huge multiplier of R&D requirements. In the data center, for example, the capacity and performance specifications for LPDDR have changed drastically, while robotics and automotive bring in advanced packaging and 3D implementations. Nearly all of these involve specific engagements with key customers, rather than simply delivering another scaled DRAM node, DeBoer said. “You can’t optimize the system without optimizing how the memory works in it.”

R&D is the price of staying competitive

Dan Hutcheson, vice chair of research firm TechInsights, has studied semiconductor R&D since the 1980s, and told EE Times in an interview that Micron’s move makes complete sense—the new lab is a way to bring in external funding and outside ideas.

Hutcheson estimated that R&D costs rise by roughly 30% with each node transition and that, in the 1980s and 1990s, costs had often increased faster than the revenues available to support them. This became less of a problem as organizations such as Sematech and imec took on shared research. Rising costs nevertheless contributed to vendor consolidation, as companies found they could no longer keep up with the investment required for the next generation.

Hutcheson distinguished between “little r, big R, little d, big D,” noting that companies are usually “big D and very little r,” especially when it comes to basic research. “It doesn’t make sense for the companies to invest in Big R because it takes 10 to 20 years for these things to mature,” he said. That’s where universities and national labs come in—and where imec has excelled. “What imec has done is a great job of bridging that gap between the university, between suppliers, and between end customers.”

AI has transformed memory from being cost-driven to being value-driven, Hutcheson said.

Research must still reach the fab

There are two key cost centers at play for memory R&D: One is developing the technology; the other is financing the manufacturing capacity needed to exploit it.

Jim Handy, principal analyst at Objective Analysis, said in an interview with EE Times that vendor consolidation is being driven by the costs of building a competitive fab, which have been rising faster than DRAM revenues.

Regardless, R&D gets its own line in a memory maker’s business model, Handy said. A DRAM manufacturer typically allocates about 20% of revenue to capital spending and about 10% to R&D. “And generally, very few layoffs happen in the R&D team,” he added.

Handy said he sees the Micron announcement partly as a repackaging of spending that would happen anyway into a 10-year commitment. “They’re pretty darn sure that they’re going to be spending that much anyway.”

The budget is also available when big AI players don’t see price as an object, Handy said. This is giving DRAM makers gross margins of 80% versus the 30% or below they are used to. More R&D should also help manufacturers advance nodes faster and squeeze more bits from existing capacity. “That will help lower the price, and that’ll be good for the buyers,” he said.

Handy stressed the value of research organizations such as imec and CEA-Leti, where companies pool their efforts to do “precompetitive” research. DRAM rivals such as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron might jointly fund a project to evaluate a new material, for example. If it pans out, they will all go off and develop their own recipes, he said. “That speaks to the incredible cost of doing this R&D.”

That model matters even more for emerging memories such as MRAM, ReRAM, and FRAM, which have spent years—sometimes decades—finding their niches rather than displacing DRAM or flash outright.

Partnerships keep emerging memories in the game

ReRAM maker Weebit Nano has relied heavily on research partnerships to bring its technology to market. CEA-Leti has been a partner from very early on, said Eran Briman, the company’s VP of marketing and business development. Weebit benefited from approximately a decade of research already undertaken by the institute before the two organizations joined forces, he said in an interview with EE Times.

Weebit Nano began working with universities and research institutes in 2018 on neuromorphic computing. In 2019, it demonstrated spiking neural networks running on its ReRAM in collaboration with CEA-Leti. In-memory compute is a nearer-term opportunity, Briman said. Compared with GPUs, CPUs, and accelerators, running AI in memory could theoretically be 10× to 100× more power-efficient, he said.

The company recently launched its Weebit Matrix In-Memory Compute (IMC) Research Program to accelerate the exploration of next-generation computing architectures. The program provides industry and academic researchers with a ReRAM-based hardware development kit to explore and prototype IMC algorithms and systems.

Through the program, researchers can use Weebit Nano’s ReRAM-based platform to develop and test AI algorithms, investigate innovative programming methods, explore new AI and neuromorphic architectures, and assess potential gains in power efficiency and performance. Participating researchers will share their ReRAM-related findings and feedback with the company to help improve the technology and contribute to the broader research community.

Research is where problems get solved, and development is implementation, Briman said. “It took a couple of decades to actually get where we are today,” he said of ReRAM’s maturity.

Commercial availability does not end that work. Customers keep requesting higher densities, greater endurance, and better performance at elevated temperatures. Briman said demands have progressed from 10,000 programming cycles to 100,000 and, for some applications, a million. AI updates, code changes, and data logging are among the drivers.

Briman said semiconductors remain a very expensive industry to play in, noting that some ReRAM vendors have tried and failed multiple times. He sees Micron’s investment as a rising tide. “There’s a ripple effect for the entire industry where we sit, and we’re going to see this coming in the next couple of years.”

Learning from failure

Memory R&D doesn’t always pay off. Micron spent billions on 3D XPoint before DeBoer killed the program earlier than its partner, Intel. “We made a decision that we had learned what we could from it.”

Bringing a new memory to market requires the technology, manufacturability, and customer acceptance, DeBoer said. “If you don’t have all three of those things worked out, it’s just not happening.”

Ultimately, Micron Research Labs reflects the company’s changing role in the semiconductor research ecosystem, DeBoer said, as memory and logic become more tightly integrated. “We intend to transform what Micron is in 10 years,” he said. “Today and going forward, this combination of memory and logic is going to be really the enabler across AI.”
