data.title: Gartner Warns of Risks Behind Sovereign Tech Claims
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

BARCELONA, Spain — Addressing enterprise and government executives at the recent Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo, Gartner analysts René Buest and Bettina Tratz-Ryan delivered a critical assessment of Europe’s campaign for digital autonomy. They warned that commercial promises of “sovereign” technology frequently amount to marketing maneuvers that leave organizations exposed to foreign jurisdiction and operational disruption.

Reinforced by Gartner research predicting that digital sovereignty will become a core component of national security strategies globally by 2030, and that over 90% of European Union organizations will adopt a sovereignty strategy by 2029, the sessions underscored an acute policy dilemma: European institutions seeking autonomy remain bound to foreign cloud giants, proprietary platforms, and offshore semiconductor manufacturing.

“As dependency risks rise, sovereignty is shifting from a question of location to an economic and operational survivability imperative,” Buest said during a conference session titled “Sovereignty Washing: How to Challenge Your Sovereign Vendor.” He added that “dependencies that once delivered efficiency must now be treated as potential business continuity risks.”

Pressures behind the autonomy debate

The renewed urgency surrounding digital sovereignty marks a departure from the previous decade, when corporate leaders consolidated workloads in centralized public clouds operated by U.S. providers, attracted by scalability, access to advanced services, and lower infrastructure management costs.

During a press briefing before the session, Buest argued that consensus has eroded amid geopolitical instability and legal confrontations. “Ten years ago, the world was a better place,” Buest said, adding that “there was more trust among nations, more trust in vendors.”

Two concerns dominate executive deliberations: unauthorized external access to data and the abrupt loss of access to critical technology. The legal exposure was underscored during French Senate testimony, when a Microsoft representative conceded under oath that the company could not guarantee that French records would remain immune from U.S. subpoenas under the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act (CLOUD Act).

While some clients were able to maintain continuity because architectures fell back on older models, the episode exposed the fragility of business processes dependent on overseas providers.

Concurrently, European institutions confront the risk of an operational cutoff, colloquially termed a “kill switch.” Buest cited cases in which geopolitical tensions altered technological access, including sanctions that severed Amsterdam Trade Bank’s access to essential technology services, restrictions disrupting systems at the International Criminal Court, and the U.S. export-control order of June 2026 that forced Anthropic to disable its Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models worldwide, before access began returning on July 1.

During the same press briefing, Tratz-Ryan outlined three competing priorities for organizations: computational performance, budgetary constraints, and jurisdictional autonomy. “Today, we’re looking at a trilemma,” Tratz-Ryan said. “We’re talking about performance, faster, more capable agents; we’re talking about cost ceilings; and then we talk about autonomy.”

Under mandates such as the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, financial entities must guarantee continuity while assessing single-point vendor dependencies. Yet because domestic sovereign alternatives remain limited in scale, enforcing sovereignty often requires duplicating technical stacks, escalating costs.

“The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale,” Tratz-Ryan warned. “The immediate priority for business and IT leaders should be strategic optionality: identifying where dependencies create unacceptable risk, where resilience is sufficient, and where managed interdependence remains the most viable option.”

The anatomy of sovereignty washing

In his conference session, Buest defined sovereignty washing as a deliberate marketing practice by IT providers that promise sovereignty while obscuring structural reasons why that commitment cannot be satisfied. “If you look behind the scenes, there’s a lot of washing going on,” Buest warned.

To assist buyers in assessing vendor claims, Buest highlighted three warning signs. The first is compliance theater, in which vendors equate encryption and regulatory checklists with genuine sovereignty. Yet technical safeguards do not shield an enterprise if systems are deactivated remotely.

The second involves nonbinding pledges and data boundary assurances that routinely yield to statutory mandates in a vendor’s home country. The third concerns ownership and architectural control: Foreign vendors advertise sovereign offerings by building local data centers while keeping ownership of core software and IP.

To clarify the technical reality, Buest displayed a slide contrasting geographic storage with operational independence: “Residency tells you where your data sleeps. Sovereignty tells you whether you can still wake it up.”

Gartner categorizes digital sovereignty into data, operational, and technological sovereignty. While local data residency addresses storage compliance, it represents the weakest tier on Gartner’s Sovereign Cloud Deployment Spectrum. Operational sovereignty requires infrastructure to be maintained independently by domestic entities, whereas technological sovereignty remains virtually unattainable for most European organizations today.

To mitigate exposure, Buest highlighted “SovereignOps,” a model that decouples service delivery from IP ownership by transferring operations to local providers under a conditional license to reduce the risk of an abrupt “kill switch” by foreign vendors.

Hardware and semiconductor chokepoint

During the press briefing, EE Times asked Buest about the physical limitations of software-centric sovereignty. Buest noted that European efforts often overlook microprocessors and network hardware, emphasizing that more than 99% of advanced computing hardware originates outside Europe, with silicon architecture dominated by American corporations such as Intel, AMD, and Nvidia. Similarly, Arm, the U.K.-based semiconductor IP company, has American executive management and is majority-owned by Japan’s SoftBank.

While European initiatives such as the DARE project pursue open-standard RISC-V-based architecture, China has made considerable progress in developing its domestic semiconductor capabilities, partly in response to U.S. export restrictions.

Buest acknowledged the vulnerability at the hardware layer. “The good news is once we have bought Nvidia or any other hardware, they typically cannot take it away from us,” Buest observed, noting that physical equipment deployed locally provides baseline operational security.

However, catching up on semiconductor fabrication presents formidable barriers. While European programs allocate funds toward design, Buest noted that allocating €500 million (~$550 million) is marginal compared to the tens of billions required to build leading-edge fabrication facilities. “There is no concrete agenda,” Buest added.

Furthermore, Buest highlighted Europe’s paradoxical position in the supply chain. Although ASML, headquartered in the Netherlands, is the world’s sole supplier of EUV lithography systems, Europe accounts for almost none of the company’s commercial revenue, which comes primarily from East Asia and North America.

“When ASML gets rogue and says we don’t sell our machines anymore, the entire AI bubble bursts immediately,” Buest noted. “Intel, TSMC, no one will be able to produce anything anymore.” Yet Buest cautioned that exercising such a lever would break the global economy.

Pragmatism over purity

Faced with structural dependencies across silicon and software, Gartner analysts advised European organizations to abandon the illusion of absolute autonomy and adopt what Buest characterized as a zero-trust approach to sovereignty. “Trust is a currency,” Buest told attendees. “Your strategy must be built on zero trust and zero tolerance: Trust no one. Question everything.”

Because enterprises cannot easily replace integrated platforms combining office software with cybersecurity and identity management, they must identify core dependencies, demand contractual exit clauses before signing, and isolate sensitive data in confidential computing environments.

True digital resilience, the analysts concluded, will not come from marketing assurances, but from an organization’s willingness to question vendor narratives and actively govern its own operational dependencies.

data.title: Nvidia Reports $115.8B in Quarterly Revenue Under Interim CEO
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, more than twice its revenue in the same period last year. Cloud providers and tech giants kept buying its AI processors at a strong pace.

This was the first financial report under interim CEO Colette Kress, who took over after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. The results show demand for Nvidia’s enterprise computing systems remains strong, even as the company faces leadership changes, a board investigation, and growing national security questions from Washington.

Rise in data center revenue

Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter and 103% from the $57.0 billion reported in the same period last year.

Most of the growth came from Nvidia’s Data Center business, which brought in $107.6 billion in sales, up 21% from the last quarter and 110% from a year ago. Gross margins stayed high, with a GAAP gross margin of 74.8% and a non-GAAP margin of 74.9%.

Operating income was $77.5 billion on a GAAP basis, up 115% from $36.0 billion a year ago. Net income grew to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per diluted share, compared to $31.9 billion, or $1.30 per share, a year earlier. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $64.9 billion, or $2.68 per diluted share. Nvidia generated $43.8 billion in free cash flow for the quarter, up from $22.1 billion in the same period last year.

Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends during the quarter. In September, the board had increased the company’s share repurchase authorization by $150 billion. At quarter-end, $227.3 billion remained available under the authorization. The board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share, payable on Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2.

Kress, who has served as Nvidia’s executive VP and CFO since 2013 and became interim CEO last week, said in the earnings release: “Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”

Vera Rubin ready for market adoption

The financial results came as Nvidia began ramping production of its next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI computing system and started shipping units to customers.

Nvidia said systems were already running at cloud providers including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. An installation was also underway with SpaceXSI.

Nvidia expanded its product lineup by shipping Vera CPUs, marking its first fully custom CPUs for data centers. Cloud platforms and AI developers such as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, and Verda have been using these custom processors with graphic accelerators to handle inference processing and automated agent tasks. For high-performance computing and complex simulations, Nvidia also introduced the Rubin HPC GPU.

The DSX POD reference design standardized how physical deployments are built, letting partners put together containerized data center modules that need less water cooling.

In networking, Nvidia rolled out more Spectrum-X Ethernet switches and BlueField-4 data processing units. The company also worked with Cisco on a new, higher-density optical transceiver called USFP. 

Beyond hardware, Nvidia announced a deal to acquire Hugging Face, an open-source platform popular with AI researchers and software engineers.

Edge computing, PCs, and robotics

Outside of central data centers, Nvidia’s Edge Computing business brought in $8.2 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 14% from the previous quarter and 42% year over year.

RTX Spark laptops began shipping through partners including ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface, and MSI.

For desktop software, Nvidia launched DLSS 5 graphics software for games. It also released a 64-GB DGX Spark personal system, supporting local execution of models from Liquid AI, Qwen, and Black Forest Labs locally.

Nvidia’s automotive and robotics segments had more deployments this quarter. Mercedes-Benz and Volvo Cars expanded their partnerships using Nvidia’s automated driving systems, and European logistics companies started testing commercial fleets built on the Hyperion vehicle platform.

The robotics division updated its Isaac platform tools to support human-sized robotic prototypes powered by Jetson Thor chips. It also worked with Nokia and T-Mobile on wireless infrastructure trials that use accelerated computing in cellular networks.

Jensen’s departure and reinstatement campaign

The company reported these results during a major management crisis. Huang resigned suddenly after internal investigations into extramarital relationships with a subordinate and an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is under federal investigation for possibly diverting regulated semiconductor hardware.

On Nov. 17, Huang made his first public remarks since stepping down, expressing remorse while leaving the door open to a return as an executive. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said in a published statement. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

A public petition called “Stand with Jensen” has collected over 202,000 signatures, including support from thousands of Nvidia employees. Industry leaders such as Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney have publicly backed Huang’s return, and shareholder groups led by Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management sent open letters asking the board to keep all leadership options open.

As of Nov. 19, the Associated Press reported that Nvidia’s board had unanimously rejected Huang’s offer to return as CEO. Board chairman Harvey Jones said the company “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”

Governance and outlook

Governance experts noted that reversing his termination could cause compliance problems with upcoming government proceedings.

Huang has agreed to appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1 to answer inquiries concerning foreign interactions and export compliance, with Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to appear the following day.

In response to the controversy, Nvidia’s board set up a special committee to oversee national security and export rules. The company has also started looking for a new permanent chief executive.

Looking ahead, Nvidia expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an extra working week. Gross margins are expected to fall to between 71.0% and 72.0%, and operating expenses should be about $11.0 billion.

Because of current export controls, Nvidia’s guidance assumes no data center revenue from China.

data.title: Koduri’s Oxmiq Offers IP, Tools for Indian Teams to Design AI Chips
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

In an exclusive interview, Raja Koduri, founder and CEO of Oxmiq Labs, discussed the company’s India initiative, the role of memory hierarchy in AI computing systems, custom silicon economics, and India’s infrastructure requirements.

Oxmiq Labs has developed tools and intellectual property (IP) to help teams in India design their own AI chips. The company is also working on an India initiative that it expects to detail in December, Koduri told EE Times.

“We have built tools to enable teams in India to make their own chips,” he said. “We are working on an initiative in India, and hopefully, when I return to India in December, I will be able to share some of those initiatives publicly.”

The aim, Koduri said, is to develop state-of-the-art chips designed to produce AI tokens as efficiently as possible.

Separately, Oxmiq is an architecture and engineering partner to AM Intelligence Labs, the AI compute division of AM Group, the parent company of Greenko, India’s renewable energy producer with a portfolio target of 50 GW by 2030. The partnership covers site selection, compute design, and partner selection. The initial build will use Nvidia GPUs, with locally developed designs to follow.

“To begin with, we are bringing the best technology available today, which is Nvidia GPUs,” he said. “But as we move toward 2030, we will also leverage designs developed in India.”

Koduri said India must develop its own designs, chips, and infrastructure to bring down the cost of converting electricity into AI output, even if manufacturing remains overseas.

“Chips designed in India can be manufactured in Taiwan or South Korea,” he said. “That is perfectly fine. But the products should be owned by India.”

From megawatts to intelligence

Koduri said the main constraint in AI computing is how efficiently a data center converts power into AI output. At the technical level, he said, the memory hierarchy matters more than floating-point operations and compute.

“It is all a memory hierarchy problem, from NAND flash storage to double data rate [DDR] memory attached to the central processing unit [CPU], high-bandwidth memory [HBM] attached to the GPU, and static random-access memory [SRAM],” he said.

A startup might focus on one type of memory, such as SRAM, and position it as the answer to a particular computing problem. But Koduri said the system-level requirements are broader.

“We look at the problem as a memory hierarchy and exploit each level as efficiently as possible,” he said.

Asked what changes when energy, compute, cooling, networking, and software are designed together, Koduri said the industry has traditionally operated in separate layers. Chipmakers typically design and sell a chip to a systems company, which builds a system. Another company builds the rack, while a data center operator handles installation, thermal management, and cooling.

“There are multiple layers in the ecosystem before everything comes together,” he said.

However, the scale of AI data center expansion is changing how companies approach the design process. Koduri said engineers must consider the entire data center rather than optimize an individual chip in isolation.

“We have to think about the whole system,” he said. “Not just the system, but the entire data center.”

The objective, he explained, is to convert incoming electricity into tokens as efficiently as possible while managing the heat generated by the chips.

Koduri described this as an optimization problem that will continue to evolve as AI models and computing architectures change. Over the past five years, he said, the industry has moved from basic transformers to mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek optimizations, and decision-making models. GPU optimization is also continuing.

“The real constraint is that we have megawatts coming in and intelligence coming out,” he said. “How efficiently can we transform those megawatts into intelligence?”

Customers, Koduri said, care about the output of the complete system. “They want to plug in electricity, provide cooling, and get tokens they can sell. That is all.”

Oxmiq’s role at AM Intelligence Labs

Oxmiq’s work with AM Intelligence Labs covers data center planning and the selection of technology partners, Koduri said.

The company’s support begins with site selection and data center design. It then works on compute design, rack placement, networking and storage requirements, thermal management, cooling, and software stack operations.

“We provide all that expertise,” he said.

“We do not necessarily solve every problem ourselves,” Koduri said. “For example, we may select a suitable partner to provide the system, such as an original equipment manufacturer. That is the kind of support we are currently providing to [AM Group], because we come from the technology world, while they come from the energy world.”

Koduri pointed to AM Intelligence Lab’s first AI factory in Hyderabad, which he described as probably the first such deployment in Asia. The company has ordered about 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for the 30-MW facility, with delivery of Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. It has since placed an additional order for 20,000 Rubin GPUs for sites in India and Malaysia.

Custom silicon economics and India’s infrastructure needs

Koduri said companies can potentially improve computing efficiency by designing the silicon, systems, and infrastructure for a specific data center rather than relying entirely on components designed for a wide range of customers.

Traditionally, a chipmaker had to sell its product to many data centers to generate revenue. That required designing a flexible product that could accommodate different customer requirements, standards, and features, even if those compromises reduced efficiency.

“If I am designing for one data center and its specific constraints, I can build something that is twice as cost-effective,” he said.

For a 1-GW data center, which Koduri estimated could cost around $55 billion to build, he said custom-designing the system could potentially deliver twice the compute by using power more efficiently.

He said this approach could change both the engineering mindset and the business model. A company developing silicon could now target the data center problem itself, with a single customer potentially generating multibillion-dollar revenue.

Koduri said custom silicon, systems, and software begin to make economic sense for customers planning at least 100 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity.

He put the cost of 100 MW of computing capacity at approximately $5.5 billion using off-the-shelf hardware. By comparison, R&D for a state-of-the-art chip manufactured by TSMC could cost around $100 million to $150 million. Developing a complete custom system could cost up to about $500 million, even with generous spending, he said.

If a custom system roughly halved that cost, a customer could save more than $2 billion even after spending $500 million on development, he said.

However, customers need the IP, tools, and technical know-how to develop custom systems, and Koduri said Oxmiq is building a solution to that problem.

Koduri said Oxmiq’s customers fall into three categories. The first comprises infrastructure companies such as AM Intelligence Labs, which are building computing capacity and need support across the system. The second includes companies designing silicon for applications such as data centers, physical AI, and enterprise AI.

Oxmiq can provide hardware and software IP to startups developing products such as chips for robots, allowing them to focus on their customers’ requirements, Koduri said.

The third category includes companies developing new materials and new physics, such as new forms of memory, silicon, silicon photonics, and photonics-based interconnects. They can license Oxmiq’s IP rather than develop the computing technology alongside their research.

In India, Oxmiq is engaging with customers in the infrastructure and silicon design categories. In the U.S., it works across all three categories, with most customers in infrastructure and new-physics applications, he said.

India’s installed data center power capacity stood at 1.57 GW in August 2026, up from about 375 MW in 2020, and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030, according to the Indian Press Information Bureau. About $70 billion of investment is underway, with a further $90 billion in announced projects.

Koduri said a 1-GW data center costs approximately $55 billion to build. By comparison, he said capital expenditure per gigawatt in China was moving toward $10 billion. “They can get things done at one-fifth, and perhaps one-tenth, of the cost of the rest of the world,” he said.

He estimated that India would need at least 6 GW of infrastructure to provide intelligence to its entire population, adding that the actual requirement would be much higher. The combined GPU capacity currently available in India, including planned deployments by AM Intelligence Labs, would not reach 100 MW, he said. That suggests India would need to increase that capacity at least 60-fold before the end of the decade.

For Koduri, the opportunity is not limited to building more data centers. It also includes developing the chips, systems, and software that convert electricity into AI output. “The opportunities for design teams, systems teams, and software teams in India are tremendous,” he said. “This is a build-out that India should participate in.”

data.title: Edge AI Moves Agricultural Intelligence from the Cloud to the Field
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

An agricultural robot moving through a field must do more than collect information: It must interpret what its sensors detect, decide what to do, and potentially act before it reaches the next plant. Sending data to a remote computer for analysis is not always practical, particularly when connectivity is unreliable or decisions must be made immediately.

Xin “Rex” Sun, director of the Peltier Institute for Advancement in Agricultural Technology at North Dakota State University, is confronting that problem in research on AI-assisted crop monitoring.

His laboratory is developing a field platform equipped with sensors that could diagnose crop problems and eventually support interventions. The research involves powerful computing systems, but Sun wants the resulting applications to run on equipment that farmers can use in their fields.

“Edge AI will be the go-to approach, because if the technology can’t run on a robot, combine, or tractor, it’s of little use to farmers,” Sun said. “Farmers aren’t sitting in laboratories doing research. They need technology that works in the field.”

His team uses Nvidia GPUs for demanding research workloads, alongside smaller computing platforms such as Raspberry Pi and Arduino for other functions. The distinction illustrates a fundamental design choice: Different tasks require different amounts and types of processing.

As agricultural machinery becomes more autonomous, equipment manufacturers must make those choices across increasingly complex systems. The challenge is no longer simply getting an AI model to recognize something; it’s giving a machine enough intelligence to respond appropriately without exceeding its power budget or compromising safety.

From sensing to acting

Nvidia’s Chen Su, head of edge AI product marketing, said in written responses to EE Times that agricultural systems are moving beyond individual applications such as crop classification, weed detection, and plant health monitoring.

“Many systems are evolving from single-purpose vision applications into multi-workload edge AI platforms that run perception, crop analysis, localization, navigation, obstacle avoidance, and control together,” Su said.

A precision sprayer, for example, must identify a target and activate the appropriate mechanism at the right moment. A more autonomous machine must also determine its location, navigate the field, detect obstacles, and coordinate its movements with the agricultural operation.

These workloads place different demands on processors. According to Su, the computing requirements depend on sensor count and type, model complexity, machine speed, reaction times, and the number of simultaneous tasks.

The need for onboard processing goes beyond the limited connectivity common in rural areas. Even with a reliable network connection, sending information to the cloud and waiting for a response can introduce unacceptable delays when a machine is moving.

Su described the architectural change as a move from “sense and report” toward “sense, decide, and act.”

That requires more capable onboard computing, sensor fusion, real-time control, and software for developing and validating autonomous systems. Nvidia’s Jetson platforms target such embedded AI workloads, where computing performance must fit within constraints on size, power consumption, heat, and cost.

Not all of the processing needs to take place in one computer. Cameras and intelligent sensors can perform image processing, compression, filtering, and some object detection locally. A more powerful central processor can combine information from multiple sensors to support navigation and planning.

The cloud remains useful for training models, simulation, fleet management, and analytics. But Su expects the principal change over the coming years to be the emergence of complete autonomy stacks running onboard agricultural machines rather than individual AI features operating in isolation.

Matching intelligence to the machine

For NXP Semiconductors, the problem is not simply how to provide more computing power; it’s how to allocate processing across the functions of an agricultural machine.

According to Ramakrishna Karamsetty, senior director of product management for edge and physical AI hardware and software products at NXP, “agriculture is one of the toughest environments for computing.”

Karamsetty, who joined NXP after more than 25 years at Intel, pointed to differences in terrain, crops, climate, and connectivity. A system developed for a farm in Arizona may encounter entirely different conditions in Idaho, China, or India. “There is no one-size-fits-all solution,” he told EE Times.

The type of agricultural operation also determines the amount of intelligence required. Harvesting corn differs from picking delicate fruit, which requires evaluating color, ripeness, and other characteristics before harvesting. “Tasks that traditionally required a person to inspect and judge the crop need more intelligence at the edge,” Karamsetty said.

That doesn’t mean every agricultural machine requires a high-performance GPU, he said. Some functions can run on microcontrollers (MCUs), while others benefit from dedicated neural processing units (NPUs) or more powerful computing platforms.

Power consumption complicates the decision. Farm equipment must operate for extended periods, and its electronics must function within available thermal and electrical limits. Karamsetty argued that performance per watt can matter more than maximizing peak computing performance.

NXP is developing discrete and integrated NPUs intended to provide appropriately sized inference capabilities. The company’s broader strategy combines application processors, AI accelerators, and MCUs rather than treating inference as an isolated function.

Karamsetty described a processing pipeline in which application processors prepare information from cameras, LiDAR, and other sensors; NPUs execute AI inference; and MCUs handle control functions.

NXP calls its approach the Neural Axis Architecture, using the human nervous system as an analogy. Different processing layers take responsibility for planning, coordinating sensor information, and executing low-latency responses. The distinction becomes particularly important when AI is responsible for operating physical machinery.

Imagine a harvester moving through a cornfield, Karamsetty said. Its vision system is identifying crops and obstacles, while other components control the harvesting mechanism, steering, and braking. If AI inference slows down or encounters a problem, the machine must still be capable of stopping safely. “Safety functions must be isolated from AI inference and normal actuator functions so that an issue or delay in one does not compromise the other,” he said.

NXP’s approach is to integrate functional safety and security capabilities with its computing architecture. The objective is to prevent a problem in perception or an agricultural operation from compromising critical machine controls.

Software integration is another priority. Karamsetty said NXP wants developers to use a common software environment across MCUs, application processors, and NPUs rather than maintaining separate optimization and deployment processes for each processor type.

Beyond the proof of concept

The ability to adapt those models may ultimately matter as much as the processors running them. Agricultural conditions vary not only between regions but also within the same field over time. Lighting, dust, fog, weather, and changing crops can all affect how an AI system interprets sensor data.

Karamsetty envisages equipment manufacturers deploying models customized for particular locations, then managing updates remotely. A machine operating in one region might need a different model from an otherwise identical machine working elsewhere.

This could help manufacturers avoid developing entirely different equipment for every crop or environment. But it also introduces the challenge of validating and maintaining models across many locations. “I think the technology is at the point where cost-effective proofs of concept are possible, but that is not the same as having fully productized, widely deployable solutions,” Karamsetty said.

Commercial deployment requires more than successful demonstrations. Manufacturers must address functional safety, security, regulatory requirements, and reliability under conditions that may differ substantially from those used to develop the original model.

There’s also a question of ownership. Agricultural AI systems may increasingly rely on data collected from individual farms to improve their performance. Karamsetty sees a potential parallel with disputes over farmers’ rights to repair their own equipment.

Similar tensions could emerge if manufacturers use farmers’ data to customize models and subsequently charge those farmers for access to the resulting intelligence. “The ability to deploy customized models will be critical, especially while respecting farmers’ data privacy,” he said.

Karamsetty expects continued improvements in computing performance per watt, greater integration, and new semiconductor architectures. But he believes the larger competitive distinction may come from how manufacturers manage software and their relationships with equipment owners.

For agricultural autonomy, more computing power is only one part of the solution. The harder task is turning that power into dependable decisions that machines can execute safely, economically, and under the unpredictable conditions of working farms.

How did a Philips spin-off that began with a machine nobody wanted become Europe’s most valuable tech company and the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools? In this video interview, EE Times talks with Marc Hijink, a technology reporter at Dutch daily NRC and author of “Focus: The ASML Way.” Hijink covered ASML for years, then got rare, independent access to the company’s sites, suppliers and customers around the world.

Hijink explains how ASML’s early reliance on outside partners such as Zeiss made it a “lightweight boxer.” The company could spread the pain of industry downturns across its supply chain and keep spending on research while competitors cut back. He also discusses the confrontational engineering culture that former CTO Martin van den Brink built on purpose. And he describes the surprising chaos that remains at a company that builds $400 million machines. The alignment among customers, suppliers and research partners that makes each new generation of lithography possible depends on globalization, Hijink said, and geopolitics is now pulling that apart.

The conversation also covers ASML’s partnership with imec, which dates back to the late 1980s. Hijink describes how a temporary High-NA EUV lab on ASML’s Veldhoven campus saved the industry about a year. He also previews his next project: Nexperia, the Chinese-owned Dutch maker of legacy chips at the center of a diplomatic clash between the Netherlands and China.

data.title: Everspin Looks to Broaden MRAM Adoption with LPDDR Standard
data.description:

Giving magnetoresistive RAM (MRAM) access to the low power DDR (LPDDR) ecosystem requires more than adapting a memory interface; it needs controller developers to have confidence there is enough customer demand to put support into silicon.

Everspin Technologies sees the development of a standard as the pathway forward. That is why Steffen Hellmold, the company’s VP of corporate strategy, is chairing a new JEDEC task group under JEDEC’s JC-42.6 Low Power Memories Subcommittee to explore an LPDDR persistent memory (PMEM) standard, he told EE Times in an interview. “If you want to have something to happen, then you need to be willing to contribute.”

Everspin’s motivation is practical because its experience adapting DDR controllers for MRAM does not translate readily to the newer LPDDR implementations it wants to target, Hellmold said.

The company’s DDR4 MRAM has been implemented in systems such as IBM’s FlashCore Module by tweaking DRAM host controllers to handle smaller page sizes and slightly different timings. Hellmold said that was workable because the controllers were soft IP. In AMD Xilinx FPGAs, for example, the memory interface generator could adapt DDR4 soft IP for MRAM.

Looking toward LPDDR5 and LPDDR6, Hellmold said the available controller implementations instead rely on hard IP, shifting those changes upstream to controller suppliers. “Hard IP means that you need to convince a host controller manufacturer to modify their host controller to also support MRAM,” he said.

IP vendors will only make that investment if there is a standard and enough customer demand, Hellmold said, but the payoff is the size of the LPDDR controller ecosystem. “If we can leverage that and slightly adapt those host controller IP blocks to work with MRAM, then we have a ubiquitous on-ramp for MRAM to easily dovetail into a much larger number of systems and applications.”

Details of the JEDEC work are confidential, Hellmold said, but he outlined three types of changes that will need to be made to achieve a standard. The proposed work involves additions, substitutions, and reductions rather than reproducing every capability of an LPDDR DRAM interface. He said MRAM does not require refresh or support for DRAM’s highest speed bins, but it does need accommodation for page sizes measured in tens or hundreds of bytes rather than kilobytes, along with somewhat longer timings.

Hellmold said these accommodations must be configurable, and that the flexibility previously available through soft IP needs to become part of what controller implementations expose to software.

For now, the JEDEC task group is an exploratory initiative, not an approved specification, aimed at leveraging existing LPDDR infrastructure while limiting changes to DRAM standards and host controllers.

Hellmold said participants in the group span edge AI, IoT, industrial, automotive, enterprise storage, and hyperscale data centers, including prospective users as well as suppliers. Even with a standard, controller IP vendors must still adopt it and get it into silicon, so he’d like to see as many potential users as possible come forward with their requirements.

There are several applications that could benefit should a standard come to fruition, Hellmold said. Everspin customers are asking for gigabyte-scale solutions, and higher-density MRAM coupled with an LPDDR persistent-memory interface would address that requirement.

Hellmold said MRAM’s trajectory puts a more cost-effective alternative to battery-backed DRAM within reach, while using MRAM as a persistent write cache ahead of NAND for checkpointing could reduce the time processors wait while preserving state. “There are tangible opportunities within line of sight,” he said.

This JEDEC initiative aligns with other efforts to broaden MRAM’s reach. Everspin recently demonstrated a 4-GB pool of CXL-attached DDR4 MRAM at the SNIA Developer Conference, which Hellmold presented as a persistent cache tier between DRAM and NAND rather than a replacement for NAND.

MRAM in the data center isn’t new either, but NOR flash shortages and AI workloads are helping to broaden its use in servers, data centers, and satellites.

data.title: Intesa Sanpaolo Finds Value Before Quantum Computers Are Ready

//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

An ATM running out of cash is a problem customers notice immediately. Keeping too much money inside it creates a quieter problem for the bank: Funds sit idle, while replenishment visits add costs. Across hundreds of machines, deciding how much cash to deliver, where, and when becomes a substantial optimization challenge.

Intesa Sanpaolo reported double-digit cost reductions from a new approach, without compromising service levels. The work emerged from the Italian banking group’s quantum computing research. The calculations, however, run entirely on classical GPUs.

That apparent contradiction gets to the heart of quantum-inspired computing. Researchers can borrow ideas from quantum algorithms and find useful ways to apply them on existing hardware. Whether a quantum processor will eventually improve on those results is a separate question.

According to Davide Corbelletto, distinguished quantum specialist and team leader of Intesa Sanpaolo’s Quantum Competence Center, what changed was the approach. “It’s a shift in the way you model the problem you’re trying to solve,” he told EE Times.

A new way of looking at the problem

Intesa selected ATM cash replenishment as a proving ground because it combined business relevance with technical suitability. Its broader outsourced network exceeds 1,000 ATMs. The bank validated the optimization system using a real network comprising hundreds of machines.

Using historical data, the team compared its approach against operational strategies and traditional optimization methods previously employed. Measures included costs, service levels, and the risk of machines running out of cash.

The team expressed the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, or QUBO, model. Decisions become binary variables, with their costs and interactions combined into an objective for a solver to optimize.

Corbelletto described quantum-inspired computing as starting with an approach conceived for quantum hardware, then reformulating it for classical execution. The adaptation may not deliver all the advantages anticipated from a future quantum implementation. It can nevertheless offer something useful today.

“But if this limited version of the solution is better than the classical one you were using, you still have a kind of advantage,” he said. “And that’s precisely what we demonstrated with the ATM cash flow optimization.”

The bank uses GPU-accelerated classical solvers. Corbelletto also identified FPGAs and specialized ASICs as possible platforms for quantum-inspired methods, depending on the application.

The reported savings establish improvement over Intesa’s previous approach. However, they don’t demonstrate quantum computational advantage or establish that a future quantum implementation will outperform the strongest classical alternatives.

Inspiration without quantum hardware

Banking is not the only area where quantum-inspired algorithms are being developed. A similar path appears in engineering research at TU Delft, although the mathematics differs.

In an interview with EE Times, Matthias Möller, a professor and applied mathematician, described composite material design as a problem involving discrete choices: Successive laminate layers can be oriented at different angles, creating a combinatorial optimization challenge.

The team he’s part of began work with a quantum algorithm and developed it into a quantum-inspired implementation using matrix product states, or MPS. He said Airbus is supporting further research to scale the initially academic work toward practical applications.

The terminology can suggest something exotic happening inside the computer. Möller offered a simpler description: “There’s no quantum magic in it. It just takes inspiration from how a quantum computer would work.”

MPS and the broader family of tensor-network techniques predate the current interest in quantum computing. Möller sees quantum research bringing renewed attention to them, including in computational fluid dynamics. Those methods can run on graphics cards or other classical hardware, although he cautioned that the CFD approaches he discussed are not production-ready.

Their usefulness must ultimately be judged against the application’s requirements. In discussing quantum algorithms, Möller argued that the benefit must be provable. That could mean faster computation or, in optimization, a guaranteed better solution.

Quantum-inspired methods offer a way to explore useful approaches on classical hardware today. Establishing where quantum computers themselves will excel remains an open research challenge, with progress needed in the algorithms as well as the machines.

“It’s not only hardware that has to evolve,” Möller said. “It’s also the algorithm or application side. There are some really hard nuts to be cracked there too.”

The whole workflow counts

For Intesa, the test begins with the ATM system. Quantum-inspired methods have already improved its cash replenishment calculations on GPUs, giving the bank a working solution against which to assess future quantum hardware. Introducing a quantum processor would require evidence of further gains across the banking process.

“Quantum hardware must demonstrate a clear end-to-end advantage in concrete optimization tasks, taking into account problem size, execution times, reliability, and integration with existing classical workflows,” Corbelletto said. For the bank, the relevant measure is whether the complete process improves.

“Preparing the data, encoding it, interfacing with classical systems, and extracting usable results may ultimately cost more than the quantum computation itself,” Corbelletto said. “Quantum computing will become commercially relevant only when the advantage survives the entire workflow and not just a benchmarked kernel of the algorithm.”

The challenge therefore extends beyond reproducing the ATM calculation on different hardware. A quantum implementation must earn its place against the available alternatives, including continuing improvements in classical optimization.

Even clearing that performance hurdle would leave another obstacle. A bank cannot build an operational dependency around a calculation that works only when experimental equipment happens to be available. Corbelletto argued that technical advances must be accompanied by sufficient capacity and dependable access.

“From an industrial perspective, the challenge lies not only in building a better quantum computer but in deploying enough of them to both guarantee high service levels for customers and comply with regulatory requirements regarding business continuity,” he said.

Classical hardware gives Intesa a route to service arrangements appropriate to its operations. Future quantum offerings must satisfy those operational requirements alongside the computational ones.

Preparing for the customer’s test

Intesa continues investigating applications spanning credit risk, fraud detection, derivatives pricing, and portfolio optimization. Corbelletto identified portfolio optimization as a candidate for nearer-term production because the team has developed a promising quantum-inspired prototype.

The bank also experiments across hardware platforms rather than selecting a presumed winning architecture. “Our starting point is always the business need rather than the hardware platform,” Corbelletto said.

Its ATM work provides a practical reason to continue. Investigating quantum methods can produce benefits before suitable quantum hardware arrives. But those benefits also establish a benchmark for the machines that follow.

“The key milestone will not be a laboratory record but a real-world banking use case where the quantum advantage survives the entire workflow, from data preparation to business outcome, and can be reproduced reliably,” Corbelletto said.

“That would be a much stronger signal than any individual hardware announcement.”

data.title: Taking a Tour of Canada’s Particle Accelerator

Canada’s particle accelerator is smaller than CERN’s flagship Large Hadron Collider, but it occupies a distinct place in the international research ecosystem: TRIUMF combines high-intensity beams, rare-isotope production, and specialized materials probes, including capabilities that advance semiconductor research.

Located on the University of British Columbia’s (UBC’s) main, forested campus in Vancouver, the research center was conceived in 1965 as the Tri-University Meson Facility, a joint initiative of UBC, Simon Fraser University, and the University of Victoria. The addition of the University of Alberta as a founding partner soon made the original name less apt. Cyclotron construction began in 1971 and was officially commissioned in 1974. Now the facility is simply known as TRIUMF and is run by a consortium of 21 member universities across Canada.

TRIUMF’s strengths lie in rare‑isotope beams, beta-detected nuclear magnetic resonance (β‑NMR), muon spin rotation (μSR), and dedicated nuclear‑astrophysics spectrometers. TRIUMF often contributes specialized detector components, accelerator technology, and computing expertise to large, international experiments, including those at CERN, while its facilities serve as Canada’s main hub for accelerator‑based science and isotope supply.

At the heart of the 13.5-acre site is the 520-MeV cyclotron, the world’s largest normal-conducting cyclotron. The machine is 18 meters across, its pinwheel-shaped magnet weighs 4,000 metric tons, and it has driven the lab’s science program since its first proton beam on Dec. 15, 1974. It accelerates negative hydrogen ions to 75% of the speed of light; a carbon foil strips away both electrons, leaving protons that are steered into beamlines running across the site to experiments and isotope-production stations.

Every year, the machine shuts down for about three months while engineers break the vacuum seal, lift the lid, and climb inside for repairs and upgrades.

Intensity, not energy

While CERN serves as the global focal point for collider-based high-energy physics, TRIUMF is a complementary, intensity-frontier laboratory. Its high-current proton and electron beams drive isotope production, materials studies, and precision nuclear and astrophysics experiments rather than multi-TeV collisions.

The cyclotron feeds the ISAC rare-isotope beamlines, while the superconducting ARIEL electron linac, the world’s highest-power e-linac for rare-isotope production, is designed to add photon-induced fission as a second rare-isotope production route. TRIUMF said ARIEL will roughly triple annual rare-isotope beam availability, from an aggregate of about 3,000 hours to 9,000 hours.

Probes, payloads, and radiation hardening

What might interest electronics engineers the most are TRIUMF’s Centre for Molecular and Materials Science (CMMS) and its Proton Irradiation Facility (PIF) and Neutron Irradiation Facility (NIF).

CMMS is home to μSR and β-NMR, condensed-matter probes that are rare, and TRIUMF claimed its specialized βw-NMR capabilities are unique. In β-NMR, beams of spin-polarized lithium-8 ions are implanted 5 to 200 nm deep in thin films and heterostructures, a capability used to study semiconductor quantum wells, superconductors, and battery materials. μSR similarly uses implanted muons as ultra-sensitive local probes of magnetism inside bulk materials.

PIF was designed primarily for single-event-effect studies and characterization of electronic components for the space environment, while NIF also serves terrestrial electronics and avionics testing. Their beams reproduce the radiation found at ground level, aircraft altitude, and low Earth orbit—but at far higher intensity, so companies can find out quickly whether, and how, their components will fail before they are committed to a launch.

Beam as currency

Getting beam time is itself an exercise in precision.

Our guide described it as “almost like a currency at the lab.” Committees allocate it, schedules are set years in advance in some cases, and they are adhered to minute by minute.

TRIUMF’s main control room is staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, blending modern readouts with older tactile tuning controls that operators still prefer. Thousands of devices are hardwired into the room. TRIUMF is developing model-assisted and machine-learning tools to reduce tuning overhead. In one reported demonstration, a beam-tuning task that took operators hours was completed in about six minutes.

A portal to big science

Canadian universities work through TRIUMF on more than 50 international collaborations and experiments, including CERN’s ATLAS experiment. ATLAS-Canada—TRIUMF and seven universities—is providing 1,500 of the approximately 7,000 silicon strip modules for the endcaps of ATLAS’s new, all-silicon Inner Tracker, being installed for the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade. The same pipeline feeds industry: Compact cyclotrons derived from TRIUMF designs produce medical isotopes in hospital basements across Canada.

For a lab whose name dates back to three founding universities, TRIUMF’s pitch today is that particle beams are national infrastructure to support science, medicine, and business, as well as a materials-and-radiation toolbox that Canada’s electronics sector would be hard-pressed to replicate.
